text: Philanthropist Edith Hooper commissioned this Baltimore house, and Marcel Breuer designed it with Herbert Beckhard. Work on site started in 1958 and finished the following year. A central courtyard divides the plan in two: living, dining, cooking and entertaining on one side, family rooms and bedrooms on the other. The front door opens onto that courtyard, where glass doors and a big rectangular gap cut into the stone back wall give an open view through the house to Lake Roland. Thick stone walls help keep noise down. Apart from the bathrooms, kitchen and family room, every room lies along the outer edge and has one wall made entirely of glass, half of it a sliding door from floor to ceiling. Facing the lake the house is glazed; its west side is a long, mostly plain wall of Maryland fieldstone.

The theatre company behind Teatro Oficina started in 1958 at the University of São Paulo's Law School. When fire destroyed its headquarters in 1966, the company staged revivals of its plays to pay for restoring the building. Lina Bo Bardi and Edson Elito designed the current theatre in 1984, and it opened in 1994. Their renovation added a walkway down the middle, 1.5 metres wide and 50 metres long, which can be entered from both the front and the back. Iron scaffolding, a structure of bare brick, planting beds and a large window all come together in the design. In 2015 The Guardian ranked it the world's best theatre for architectural design. Since the 1980s the company has been in conflict with Grupo Silvio Santos about residential towers planned for the neighbouring land.

Kiyonori Kikutake built the Sky House in Tokyo in 1958 as his own home. On its hillside site, a platform rests on four concrete panels beneath a shell roof shaped as a hyperbolic paraboloid. The interior is one open room, split up by storage units, while the kitchen and bathroom sit along the outer edge. Both of these were meant to be movable, so they could be shifted as the use of the house changed. Kikutake worked on it with the structural engineer Gengo Matsui, who partnered with him on more than 40 buildings. At CIAM '59 in Otterlo, the final CIAM meeting, Kenzo Tange presented the house alongside Kikutake's Tower-shaped City. Louis Kahn, after his lecture on 13 May, was invited to the house and spoke at length there with Japanese architects, the Metabolists among them.

The Fredensborg Houses are a housing estate in Denmark that Jørn Utzon designed for Danes who had spent long periods working abroad. Dansk Samvirke invited him to create a place where returning pensioners could live together and share their experiences. The scheme grew from a 1953 competition project, inspired by Danish farmhouses set around a courtyard and by Chinese architecture: each home opens onto a central court but is shielded from the outside by its outer wall. Utzon worked additively, starting with one unit and growing from it while following the lie of the land. The estate mixes courtyard homes and terraced houses with a central building holding a restaurant, meeting rooms and guest rooms. On a slope and facing south-east or south-west, the houses all get plenty of light. His additive approach had a considerable influence on later developments.

Baker House, at 362 Memorial Drive in Cambridge, is a co-ed dormitory at MIT. Alvar Aalto designed it in 1947–1948, after coming back to MIT once the war was over, and it was built in 1949. Set along the Charles River, its wavy plan gives every resident as much view and ventilation as possible. With it, Aalto began his red-brick period. Brick here was his nod to the tradition of Ivy League universities, and he later used the material for several important buildings at home in Finland, above all a number at Helsinki's new University of Technology. To mark fifty years, the dormitory was renovated in 1999: its plumbing, telecommunications and electrical systems were updated, and later interior alterations that had not been part of Aalto's design were taken out.

Cocoa House is a skyscraper by The Plan Group (West Africa) in Dugbe, a major business district of Ibadan, Nigeria. Chief Obafemi Awolowo started the project in the late 1950s under the Western Region Development Plan, and its first name was Ìlé Àwọn Àgbẹ̀, meaning "House of Farmers". Money from the region's farm produce, including cocoa, rubber and timber, paid for it. Because cocoa exports had funded it, the tower was renamed Cocoa House, and a cocoa tree was planted out front next to a fountain. Finished in July 1964 and commissioned a year later, it stands 105 metres tall. It was West Africa's first skyscraper and remained Nigeria's tallest building until 1979. A fire gutted it in January 1985; once renovated, it returned to commercial use in 1992, and today major firms and broadcasters have offices there.

BedZED (Beddington Zero Energy Development) is an eco-friendly housing scheme in Hackbridge, London. Its architect, Bill Dunster, designed it to be carbon neutral. Built between 2000 and 2002, it contains 82 homes along with 1,405 square metres of space for work. It was the first project in which a local authority sold land for less than market value so that sustainable development could be made to pay. Residents used about 3 kWh of electricity per person each day, a quarter below the UK average, and solar panels supplied 11% of it. Some parts fell short: the "Living Machine", meant to recycle water, could not clean it well enough. In 2003 the scheme made the Stirling Prize shortlist, and judges of the RIBA Journal sustainability award commended it for questioning how people both live and work.

Crow Island School, in Winnetka, teaches children from kindergarten through fourth grade. The Chicago firm Perkins, Wheeler & Will designed it with Eliel and Eero Saarinen, and it was established in 1940–41. Known for its progressive philosophy, it was among the first North American schools in the International Style. The designers asked pupils and teachers for their views and attended lessons. Its site, Crow Island, is raised ground in the Skokie Marsh, built up with fill from two Works Progress Administration projects. Four wings reach out from a central block of shared rooms, giving each classroom its own outdoor courtyard. The single storey is flat apart from a 15-metre chimney on the north side, a vertical "fifth wing". In 1971 it received the AIA's Twenty-five Year Award, and in 1990 it was named a National Historic Landmark.

Charles and Ray Eames built this mid-century modern house in Los Angeles in 1949 for themselves. It belonged to the Case Study House Program, which John Entenza launched in Arts & Architecture magazine in 1945. With Eero Saarinen, the couple first proposed a raised, L-shaped structure, then reworked it into two separate rectangular pavilions, one a residence and one a studio, built of various materials. As House 8 in the series, it was completely redesigned from its original plan, for reasons still disputed. Construction started in 1948, and in 1949 the frame went up in a day and a half. The residence lies to the south of a central courtyard and the studio to the north. Both pavilions sit on a hillside along the western edge of the site, leaving the rest to trees and a meadow.

In central Harare, Zimbabwe, Eastgate Centre combines shops and offices. Mick Pearce designed it and Ove Arup and Partners built it. Pearce drew on the termite mound, which holds a steady temperature despite wide swings between night and day. Two rows of commercial space, nine storeys high, line an atrium roofed in glass; shops take the lowest two levels and offices fill the rest. Forty-eight brick funnels serve every office and shop, pulling cool air up from the basement and releasing hot air at the top. The passive system collects cool air at night and spreads it inside by day, while heavy concrete walls reduce heat gain from the sun. Patterns in the masonry echo the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe. Reports say it uses only a tenth of the energy of a comparable building with conventional cooling.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this house, built 1946–1948, for Herbert Jacobs, a journalist, and his wife Katherine, a decade after designing their first home. The name reflects its plan, an arc of a semicircle, plus its natural materials and energy-saving orientation. The couple turned down Wright's first scheme; this second one is set partly into an earthen berm. On the north side, built partly into the berm, rises a round stair tower faced in stone; on the south, a curved glass wall looks onto a sunken garden. A tunnel through the berm forms the entrance. Above the berm, a slim strip of clerestory windows lets light and summer air into the back. Horizontal limestone slabs, alternately projecting and recessed, resemble natural outcrops. Contractor delays and a misunderstanding led Wright to resign, and the Jacobses built much of it themselves.

Spa Green Estate lies in Clerkenwell, London, between St John Street and Rosebery Avenue. Berthold Lubetkin and Tecton designed it first in 1938 and reworked it in 1943; it is the fullest post-war realisation of a 1930s plan to renew society through Modernist architecture. Lubetkin intended it as a manifesto, both exciting and rational, and said: "we will deliberately create exhilaration". Working families got features of his luxury Highpoint flats, such as lifts, central heating, balconies and a roof terrace. Ove Arup's concrete box-frame, or "egg-crate", structure gave every flat open views and rooms without beams, columns or pipes. A plaza with a nursery school lies between two parallel eight-storey blocks, and Sadler House curves between the plaza and the older terraced houses on Rosebery Avenue. Listed Grade II* in 1998, the estate had its original colours restored in 2008.

The entrances to the Bilbao Metro, known as "fosteritos", are glass structures named after their designer, Norman Foster. Foster and partners won the station design in an open competition in 1988, and the system opened in 1995. Each station is dug as a large cavern with a cross-section of 160 square metres, giving one big open space instead of the usual chain of linked tunnels. The ticket area shares this volume with the trains, on steel "mezzanines" built over the tracks, and lifts and escalators make the trains fully accessible. Steel and concrete are used throughout. Sarriko station breaks the pattern: in place of a fosterito, a vast glazed atrium floods the whole station with daylight, over a long, unbroken escalator ride down to the ticket hall. It won the 1998 Brunel Award for Railway Design.

The Mesa Laboratory was built for the National Center for Atmospheric Research on Table Mesa in Boulder, beneath the sandstone cliffs of the Flatirons. I. M. Pei designed it in 1961, his first project beyond urban building design. Drawing on the Anasazi cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde, he used geometric forms, bush-hammered concrete and a pinkish local aggregate so the complex would blend into the hills. In revision, a single tall tower became a village-like cluster of three five-storey towers, built in two stages to keep within the National Science Foundation's budget. A maze-like plan was meant to make scientists meet. Finished in 1966 and dedicated a year later, it suffered from leaking roofs and circulation problems, yet received the Laboratory of the Year award in 1967 and the 25 Year Award from the AIA's Colorado chapter in 1997.

On a steep hillside in Pomona, on land once considered unusable, stands Diamond Ranch High School. Morphosis and Thomas Blurock Architects designed it in an expressionist modern style, with Morphosis's Thom Mayne in charge. District voters passed a school improvement bond worth $62.5 million in June 1991, earmarking around $10 million of it for Diamond Ranch. Morphosis was hired by the district in November 1993. Students arrived on 5 September 1997, before building work had finished. The design was recognised in a book titled Morphosis/Diamond Ranch High School. Its modernist architecture, its size and its California setting have made the campus a film location for Serenity, The Cell, Live Free or Die Hard, Orange County and The Thinning, among others.

Frank Gehry designed this Los Angeles office building, finished in 1991, for the advertising agency Chiat/Day, and it was first called the Chiat/Day Building. Its nickname comes from Giant Binoculars, a public artwork from 1991 by Coosje van Bruggen and Claes Oldenburg that stands on the facade facing the street. Beneath the sculpture are an entrance for cars and one for pedestrians, and the route into the parking garage runs between its two telescopes. The building measures about 7,000 square metres; its construction was held up for a few years when hazardous materials turned up on the site and had to be cleared away. Google moved in as tenant in 2011 and took over two neighbouring buildings in a large expansion aimed at growing its Los Angeles workforce.

Salvador's main cultural centre, Solar do Unhão, was once a sugar mill. Its name recalls Pedro Unhão Castelo Branco, a high court judge of the 17th century. Invited by Bahia's governor to lead a new art museum for the North East, Lina Bo Bardi converted the mill into a modern art museum between 1959 and 1963. Her approach to old buildings was to restore them while avoiding both nostalgia and disregard for their context; here she left the colonial exterior untouched and inserted a modern staircase. The museum was to display the primitive art of the North East and the practical character of its design. Bo Bardi saw a museum not as a mausoleum for the past but as an active place of knowledge, and in its early years it offered locals many classes in art and history.

Finished in 2001, the primary school at Gando, Burkina Faso, was the village's first primary school and Diébédo Francis Kéré's first building. It was funded via today's Kéré Foundation, whose original name roughly means "Building Blocks for Gando". Schools in Burkina Faso are usually concrete, costly and intolerably hot inside; Kéré built with mud bricks of local earth instead. A wide, raised tin roof keeps rain off the walls and lets air move beneath for cooling. He drew plans in the sand for villagers, many unable to read, who fully engaged. He aimed to join what he had learned in Europe with traditional ways of building. In 2004 the school won an Aga Khan Award for Architecture. A 2012 library addition, built with local help, lights its reading room through dozens of bottomless clay pots set into the roof.

The Salk Institute stands on the Torrey Pines Mesa in La Jolla, on land San Diego granted after Salk and Louis Kahn asked for it in March 1960 and a referendum approved it that June. Salk wanted a beautiful campus to draw the world's best researchers. Kahn planned three clusters, for meetings, living and laboratories, but only the laboratories were built: two symmetric wings either side of a travertine-paved plaza. The two blocks frame a long view of the Pacific, accentuated by a thin linear fountain running towards the ocean. After two years, Kahn and the Institute switched from four narrow laboratory buildings of two floors to two wider ones of three. No walls divide the laboratories on any floor, to encourage collaboration. August Komendant re-engineered the structure and trained the builders to produce a highly refined concrete finish.

Oscar Niemeyer designed this chapel in Pampulha, Belo Horizonte, in an organic modern style, with the mayor, Juscelino Kubitschek, as patron. Moving away from slabs on columns, Niemeyer built a parabolic concrete vault, a shape used until then only for hangars. Four wavy concrete parabolas act as both structure and enclosure, so the church needs no masonry. Outside, pastel ceramic tiles in light blue and white make abstract designs, joined by art panels from Candido Portinari and Paulo Werneck; inside hang Portinari's 14 panels of the Stations of the Cross. The landscape is by Roberto Burle Marx. Finished in 1943, the building was only consecrated in 1959: for 14 years, church authorities under the Archbishop of Belo Horizonte would not let it hold Catholic services. It was the first modern architectural monument to be listed in Brazil.

Giancarlo De Carlo designed this neighbourhood in Terni between 1969 and 1974 for 3,000 workers of Società Terni Acciaierie. The New Brutalist concrete complex is known for how much its future residents shaped the design. Over a thousand people joined meetings, interviews and debates, and a 1970 exhibition of models from around the world showed possible designs. The houses vary in size and are connected by a network of stairs, gardens and corridors. De Carlo used it to test his theory of popular participation and as a response to the Monte Amiata housing in Milan by Carlo Aymonino, though he wanted a low-rise, high-density plan while the sociologist De Mesi wanted residents shaping every part. It was only partly built: there was opposition from the old village, and work stopped for good when Gianlupo Osti left the company's presidency.

The Michael Lee-Chin Crystal, a deconstructivist, crystalline structure, is the centrepiece of the Royal Ontario Museum's expansion in Toronto. In an international competition, Daniel Libeskind's design was selected from 50 finalists. Opened in 2007, the Crystal replaced the Queen Elizabeth II Terrace Galleries and gave the museum a new entrance with sliding doors on Bloor Street. Its tilted walls stop before the older heritage buildings, and the envelope is closed between the new shape and the old walls. A three-storey atrium, the Hyacinth Gloria Chen Crystal Court, serves as the main lobby. Inside are seven further galleries, a cafeteria, a gift shop and the largest temporary exhibition hall of any museum in Canada. It recalls other Libeskind works, above all Berlin's Jewish Museum. It drew controversy, and reports in October 2007 said it was leaking badly.

Luis Barragán lived in this Mexico City house until his death in 1988, altering it often as a laboratory for his ideas. Its plain street facades of rough cement closely match the neighbours in colour and composition. The house turns inward instead, centred on a garden enclosed by high walls on every side but the west. Floor levels vary, as do room heights. Apart from the breakfast nook, the house needs no artificial light by day, because windows and openings are placed to admit as much light as possible. The colours draw on the bright tones of traditional Mexico, tempered by the artists Rufino Tamayo and Jesús Reyes Ferreira. Its influences are mostly Mexican, partly international. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 2004 as one of the most influential and representative works of modern Mexican architecture.

Foster and Partners designed Bloomberg London with the structural engineer AKT II, and Sir Robert McAlpine built it for £1bn. Two buildings are divided by a covered arcade and linked by bridges; lined with restaurants, the arcade revives a stretch of Watling Street, an old Roman road. The facades use 9,600 tonnes of sandstone from Derbyshire, set with bronze fins for ventilation. Placing the cores outside leaves one open-plan space inside. Floors are connected by custom glass lifts and a bronze ramp that spirals for 210 metres. In the lobby, three curved timber shells form a self-supporting "vortex"; express lifts climb from there to a sixth-floor pantry of double height that looks out to St Paul's Cathedral. Under the BREEAM sustainability assessment it scored 98.5%, the highest design-stage rating achieved by any major office development.

Standing at the corner of Borgesiusstraat and Abraham Kuyperlaan in Rotterdam's Bergpolder district, the Bergpolderflat was the Netherlands' first gallery flat. Willem van Tijen designed it in 1933–1934 together with Brinkman and Van der Vlugt, using a functional Modern style intended to look sleek, light and airy. Its steel skeleton supports nine floors holding 72 homes, each entered from an access gallery. The floors pair traditional timber beams with a fireproof concrete floor in three layers. Critics noted how few bedrooms there were; Van Tijen replied that the flats were meant mostly for young, modern people who enjoy simplicity, light and space. It is a national monument and was renovated in 1996.

Raymond Hood, lead architect of Rockefeller Center in New York City, designed this Art Deco skyscraper, finished in 1933 with 66 storeys and a height of 260 metres. It is massed in three parts: the main tower on the east, a nine-storey central block without windows that held NBC's studios, and a 16-storey annex on the west. Following the 1916 Zoning Resolution, the building is largely a slab, and its setbacks serve mainly for visual effect. Limestone covers the facade above a granite base, and some 6,000 windows are separated by aluminium spandrels. Bronze-and-glass doors at the main entrance stand below a cast-glass wall by Lee Lawrie. According to the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat, its massing signalled a new, slab-like kind of skyscraper, and Goldberger described its form as "made sumptuous by its mounting setbacks".

The Louvre-Lens brings works from the Paris Louvre to Lens, part of an effort to give people outside Paris access to French cultural institutions. Its 20-hectare site, a mine closed in the 1960s, was chosen to help revive a depressed mining community; officials took inspiration from the "Bilbao effect" of Bilbao's Guggenheim, though some locals found the project patronising. SANAA won a worldwide contest with Imrey Culbert, the landscape architect Catherine Mosbach and the museographer Studio Adrien Gardère. To blend into its setting, the museum is a string of five low buildings: a square glass-walled centre and rectangular wings in polished aluminium that blur their surroundings in reflection. A central building flanked by wings echoes the Paris Louvre. In the 3,000-square-metre Galerie du Temps, about 200 works stand in one open hall in date order, whatever their style or origin.

Paul Wallot's Neo-Renaissance Reichstag, built 1884–1894, housed the legislature of the German Empire and the Weimar Republic. The 1933 fire damaged it so badly that the parliament moved to the nearby Kroll Opera House. Partly restored in the 1950s, it hosted exhibitions and events, since its place in West Berlin ruled out use as a parliament. From 1995 to 1999 Norman Foster redesigned it as the permanent parliament of reunified Germany. The building was gutted to its outer walls, but traces of history had to stay visible, including bullet holes and graffiti left by Soviet soldiers in 1945. A large glass dome gives a 360° view of the city and looks down into the debating chamber, sending daylight to the floor below, while an electronically tracking sun shield blocks direct sunlight that would cause heat gain and glare.

Foster & Partners designed the Commerzbank Tower in Frankfurt, with Arup and Krebs & Kiefer as structural engineers. In the early 1990s the city's Green Party urged the bank to build "green", and the result was called the world's first ecological skyscraper. The plan is a rounded equilateral triangle, 60 metres wide, around a central triangular atrium. At nine levels the atrium opens to one side, forming large sky gardens that let in daylight and cut the need for artificial lighting, while offices on the other two sides look onto the city or a garden. To keep columns out of the sky gardens, the tower was built in steel rather than cheaper concrete, the first German skyscraper with steel as its main material. It holds 121,000 square metres of offices with winter gardens, daylight and natural ventilation.

Richard Meier designed the €20 million building for Museum Frieder Burda, which opened in Baden-Baden in 2004. Frieder Burda had first intended to put his museum near Mougins in France, where he owned a house, before choosing this town. The museum is a glass and aluminium volume of two storeys, placed at the edge of the town's main park. Huge trees rise above it, historic oaks and a blood beech among them. A bridge clad in glass joins it to the Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden, the town's small existing art museum, so the new gallery and the older one are linked. In 2006 the building received an Honor Award for Architecture from the American Institute of Architects.

Christian de Portzamparc designed Paris's Cité de la Musique, opened in 1995, along with the neighbouring Conservatoire de Paris. One of the Grands Projets of François Mitterrand, it helped to reinvent La Villette, once the city's slaughterhouse district. The complex contains exhibition halls, workshops, a music library, a music museum, an amphitheatre and a concert hall that seats 800 to 1,000. The museum's collection, first opened to visitors in 1864, moved here in 1997; its instruments span the sixteenth century to today and come from non-European, modern and Western classical music. In 2015, when Jean Nouvel's larger symphony hall, named Philharmonie 1, was built, the complex was renamed Philharmonie 2 within the Philharmonie de Paris.

Juan O'Gorman bought a plot with two tennis courts in San Ángel, a colonia of Mexico City, in 1929. There he put up a small studio and house for his father to use, today called the Cecil O'Gorman House. O'Gorman described it as Latin America's first functionalist structure. His contemporary Diego Rivera was impressed by the design and then asked him to build a home for Rivera and Frida Kahlo on the neighbouring plot. Kahlo and O'Gorman were already acquainted, having been friends from their high school days in Coyoacan.

Raj Rewal designed this New Delhi building, also known as Jawahar Vyapar Bhawan, for the State Trading Corporation of India, a government-owned company. Its construction ran from 1976 to 1989, and it is seen as a significant example of modernist architecture in India after Independence. Rewal borrowed from Japanese Metabolism yet departed from it by turning to Mughal architecture, which shows most clearly in his choice of polychromatic sandstone cladding rather than concrete. The design is called "structurally expressive" and uses Vierendeel trusses. Along with offices, the building contains a government-run store selling Indian crafts, the Central Cottage Industries Emporium.

Built in 2003 for UEFA Euro 2004, Braga Municipal Stadium was cut from the Monte do Castro quarry above the city, and so it is nicknamed A Pedreira, "The Quarry". Its design helped earn Eduardo Souto de Moura the Pritzker Architecture Prize. Stands run along both sides of the pitch, and the rock face of the quarry closes one goal end. Each stand has a canopy-style roof, and the two are tied by dozens of steel cables, inspired by ancient Incan bridges. People move between the stands through a 5,000-square-metre plaza beneath the pitch. The enormous job of moving rock contributed heavily to a final cost of €200 million, against an estimate of €29.9 million, making it the costliest of the ten new Euro 2004 stadiums. In 2006 it received the International Architecture Award of the Chicago Athenaeum.

On Punta Massullo, on Capri's east side, Casa Malaparte stands on a cliff that rises 32 metres from the sea and faces the Gulf of Salerno. Curzio Malaparte conceived it around 1937 and built it himself, helped by Adolfo Amitrano, a local stonemason. The house is a box of red masonry; a stair shaped like an inverted pyramid climbs to a patio on the roof. You can walk there from Capri town, or come by boat and climb a staircase carved into the cliff. The house, especially its roof patio, features strongly in Contempt (Le Mépris), the 1963 film by Jean-Luc Godard. When Malaparte died in 1957 the house was abandoned; it was vandalised and exposed to the weather for years, and it was badly damaged before its first serious renovation, between the late 1980s and the early 1990s.

Henri Labrouste built the new reading room of the Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève in Paris between 1838 and 1851; it was the first in Paris built specifically as a library. It shows the influence of the beaux-arts style, Florence and Rome, with a Roman-like base, simple arched windows and discreet bands of sculpture. The facade is exactly as long as the reading room, and its large windows express its function. The plan is simple: stacks, rare books and offices below, and a central vestibule and stair leading up to a reading room that fills the whole upper storey. There, the iron frame is left on show: sixteen slender cast-iron Ionic columns split the room into twin aisles and carry openwork iron arches holding plaster barrel vaults reinforced with iron mesh. Modernists revere it for bringing high technology into a monumental building.

Mario Botta designed the Cymbalista Synagogue in Tel Aviv in 1996, and it was built in 1997–1998. On a plan of about 800 square metres, two matching towers rise from a rectangular base. Each begins square and turns into a circle at its top, 13.5 metres up, and a rectangular lobby joins the two. In these towers the geometric problem of squaring the circle is made real in stone. At the round top of each tower, a square "canopy" drapes daylight down the walls of the hybrid volume, part cylinder and part box. These canopies recall the chuppah, the traditional Jewish wedding canopy, here made permanent and cast in light. Translucent onyx partly lights the Torah Ark. In 2022 the Council for the Conservation of Heritage Sites in Israel declared the building a protected heritage site.

Marcel Breuer designed this house in New Canaan, Connecticut, as a home for his family. He had moved his office to New York City in 1946, and land in New Canaan was cheaper than in the city. The house is an early example of his "long house" or "long box" designs, shaped by Bauhaus principles and later refined in Breuer House III on Cape Cod. Here he experimented with balloon framing: it is a wooden structure whose upper storey cantilevers outward, carried by steel suspension cables. The main rooms are upstairs, bedrooms to the south and family rooms to the north, placed to catch low winter sun and morning light. Its cantilevered form, finished in glass, wood and stone, drew attention to his young practice, though extra walls later added against sagging have blunted the effect.

Built in 857 AD under the Tang dynasty, the East Hall, or Dongda Hall, is the main hall of Foguang Temple in Wutai and the third earliest preserved timber structure in China. A woman, Ning Gongyu, paid most of its cost, and the monk Yuancheng led construction. Because of its hillside site, the temple faces west rather than south like most Chinese temples. Its buildings climb three terraces from west to east. The highest, raised about 13 metres on a massive stone retaining wall, carries the hall, which looks west across the valley. The hall is a single storey, seven bays by four (34 by 17.7 metres), on inner and outer sets of columns. It alone unites Tang architecture, sculpture, mural painting and calligraphy in one building, the "Four Supremacies". Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin rediscovered the temple in 1937.

This auditorium in Tempe is considered one of Frank Lloyd Wright's last public commissions. In 1956 a roof collapse left the university's combined auditorium and gymnasium unusable, and in 1957 President Grady Gammage set out to give the campus a new hall. His friend Wright based the design, with budget-related changes, on a circular opera house he had conceived for Baghdad. Both men died in 1959; William Wesley Peters, Wright's protégé, completed the building, built from 1962 to 1964. Fifty concrete columns hold up the circular roof, patterned with interlocking circles, and twin "flying buttress" ramps, 61 metres long, reach from its north and east sides to the parking lot. The stage adapts to opera, theatre, musicals, concerts and lectures. In 1985 it was added to the National Register of Historic Places.

The Cameron Offices in Canberra are former government offices designed by John Andrews for the National Capital Development Commission and built between 1970 and 1976 in a brutalist structuralist style. They were the first major buildings in Belconnen, part of a town plan for a compact, pedestrian-oriented scheme following the slope towards the man-made Lake Ginninderra. Andrews, then teaching at the University of Toronto, came home for the job, seeking a truly Australian large-scale modern building. Much of the Mall was cast in place, while the office wings were precast on site, mostly post-tensioned. It won worldwide acclaim through a listing on the Union of International Architects Heritage register. Yet voids within the wings caused wind-tunnel effects that made it unpleasant to walk around. Only three of the nine wings and the pedestrian bridge remain, two now student housing.

Robarts Library is the University of Toronto's main humanities and social sciences library. The brutalist tower rests on an equilateral triangle with 100-metre sides, the length of a Canadian football field, and triangular patterns run throughout; from the southeast corner it looks like a peacock. Mathers & Haldenby led the design, consulting the New York firm Warner, Burns, Toan & Lunde, specialists in precast concrete. Built from 1968 to 1973, its plan grew by three storeys during the Canadian Centennial celebrations. It has fourteen storeys over two underground floors, with a suspended fourth floor. The concrete is smooth in horizontal bands and rough in vertical ones, and steel-framed bay windows recall the overhanging towers of medieval castles. A mezzanine links it to the Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library and the Claude T. Bissell Building, forming a three-tower complex.

Rovaniemi Library is the main public library of the Finnish city of Rovaniemi, designed by Alvar Aalto and completed in 1965. The earlier library was destroyed in the Lapland War, along with up to 90% of the city's buildings, and the centre had to be rebuilt. Aalto's 1946 "Reindeer Antler Plan" lays out five arterial roads in the shape of an antler. At its heart, the library forms the "Aalto Centre" with the Lappia Hall and the city hall, a group protected as a nationally important built cultural environment. The building pairs a long, rectangular office wing with a central fan-shaped space for lending and reading. The reading areas sit in a sunken "reading well", a signature of many Aalto libraries, while extensive roof lights let daylight fall on the shelves along the inner walls.

Teatro Colón, a historic opera house in Buenos Aires, replaced a theatre opened in 1857. Its cornerstone was laid in 1889 under Francesco Tamburini and Vittorio Meano, his pupil, who gave it an Italian-style design. Work then stalled because of money problems, disputes over the site, Tamburini's death in 1891, the death of its financier Angelo Ferrari, and Meano's murder in 1904. Julio Dormal, a Belgian architect, completed it, altering parts of the structure and giving the decoration a French feel. After 20 years of work it opened with Verdi's Aïda on 25 May 1908. The facade's busts and bas-reliefs are by the sculptor Luigi Trinchero. In acoustician Leo Beranek's survey of leading directors, it ranked first in the world for opera acoustics and second for concerts. In 1989 it was declared a National Historic Monument.

Designed by Oscar Niemeyer and engineered by Joaquim Cardozo, the Cathedral of Brasília was completed and dedicated on 31 May 1970. It is a hyperboloid structure made of 16 concrete columns, each weighing 90 tons. Between them sit 16 fibreglass pieces, each 10 metres wide at the base and 30 metres long, and beneath these hangs a 2,000-square-metre stained glass work made by Marianne Peretti in 1990. A reflecting pool, 12 metres wide and 40 centimetres deep, surrounds the roof and helps cool the building. Visitors enter through a tunnel that passes under this pool and emerge into a bright space beneath the glass roof. Three angel sculptures hang over the nave on steel cables. The cathedral holds up to 4,000 people, and four bronze Evangelists by Alfredo Ceschiatti and Dante Croce stand in the square outside.

Kenzo Tange designed the Supreme Court Building in Islamabad in a modernist style that complements the Parliament Building nearby. It stands on Constitution Avenue, with the Prime Minister's Office on its southern side and, to its north, the Parliament Building and the Presidential Palace. Its construction was long, running from the 1960s, with the CDA's engineering department and the Environmental Protection Agency supervising the monument and its civil works. The court complex covers 339,861 square feet and is made up of three parts: a Main Central Block, a Judges' Chambers block and an Administrative Block. Its parts include judges' chambers, a law library, a range of meeting spaces and support services, including a lecture auditorium.

Eileen Gray, an architect and furniture designer from Ireland, designed and built E-1027 at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin with the architect Jean Badovici between 1926 and 1929. The name encodes the pair: E for Eileen, 10 for Jean, 2 for Badovici and 7 for Gray. With its L-shaped plan, flat roof, floor-to-ceiling glazing and a spiral stair up to the guest room, the house is open yet compact. It is seen as Gray's first major work, blurring architecture and decoration and shaped around how its intended occupants would live. Gray also made furniture for it, among it a tubular steel table whose adjustable top caught crumbs. Le Corbusier painted vivid murals on the white walls in 1938 and 1939, which Gray regarded as vandalism. After a long restoration, the house opened to visitors in July 2021.

Benjamin Britten conducted the opening concert of the Queen Elizabeth Hall in 1967. This South Bank music venue in London was built for the Southbank Centre alongside the smaller Purcell Room. A Greater London Council team designed both auditoriums: Hubert Bennett led it, working with Geoffrey Horsefall, F. G. West and Jack Whittle. So as not to rival the Royal Festival Hall in scale and presence, the design expresses the building's separate masses and elements. The vee-shaped foyer is raised to first-floor level on octagonal columns of reinforced concrete and connects to the auditorium through cast concrete tubes that recall a spaceship docking. The auditorium is a separate building, its seating cantilevered toward the foyer on a massive column that contains the escape stairs. Sparing in decoration, it is brutalist work that brings out the plasticity of concrete.

John Lautner designed this modernist house in Los Angeles in 1960 for a site so steep, with a 45-degree slope, that it was thought practically unbuildable. His answer was a one-storey octagon of around 2,200 square feet perched on a concrete column about 1.5 metres wide and nearly 9 metres high. A buried concrete pedestal almost 6 metres across supports the column, and because of it the house has survived earthquakes and heavy rain. The house is reached by a funicular. Inside, a central wall of exposed brick with a fireplace bisects the plan. The client, aerospace engineer Leonard Malin, had been given the lot by his father-in-law. The $140,000 cost was partly subsidised by barter with two sponsoring companies; one of them, Chem Seal, supplied experimental coatings and resins and inspired the house's name.

Popularly called 'The Pot', this Rotterdam building is an art depot for Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, designed by the Dutch firm MVRDV. Its form is a bowl 39.5 metres high, inspired by an aluminium-coloured IKEA bowl, and its surface is covered in more or less continuous reflective plates that mirror the surroundings back at a smaller scale. On the side facing the adjacent Erasmus MC, some plates have been made matt to guarantee the privacy of its patients. Inside, over 151,000 objects share fourteen storage compartments set to five different climates. The museum's previous storage space suffered severe flooding in 2013. The first pile for the new depot went into the ground on 17 March 2017.

Dublin's Custom House is an 18th-century neoclassical building, today home to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. John Beresford, who in 1780 became Ireland's first commissioner of revenue, came up with the project. When the original architect, Thomas Cooley, died, Beresford appointed James Gandon in 1781, giving him his first large-scale commission. Opposition was strong: Dublin Corporation and some merchants objected that it moved the city's axis, left shipping little space and stood on land that was then a swamp, and a mob of several thousand disrupted the laying of the foundations. Beresford ignored the protests. Gandon chose Irish artists as assistants, among them stone-cutter Henry Darley, and every available mason in the city was engaged. Coats of arms decorate all four facades, along with sculptures by Edward Smyth that stand for the rivers of Ireland.

In Hamar, Norway, the Hedmark Museum is a regional museum whose grounds include the medieval Cathedral Ruins mentioned in Sigrid Undset's Kristin Lavransdatter. The building called Storhamarlåven started out as a 17th-century barn of the Storhamar farm, standing next to the ruins. Sverre Fehn reworked it in concrete, wood and glass, materials picked to set it apart from the medieval stone. His aim was to bring out both layers of history: the medieval structure and the later farm building. Ramps carry visitors up so they can view the museum from above. In 1976 the design received the Betongtavlen architectural award. The cathedral ruins themselves now sit under a glass shelter by Lund & Slaatto Architects, completed in 1998.

Henry van de Velde, a painter, architect and interior designer from Belgium, built the Villa Bloemenwerf in Brussels in 1895 as his home, and it was his first work as an architect. He designed the house, its interiors and its furniture, drawing partly on William Morris's Red House in Bexleyheath. His reach went further still: he created textiles, wallpaper, silverware and even clothing to match the style of the house. His wife, Maria Sèthe, designed the garden around it. Besides being the family home, the villa served as a workshop for van de Velde and his collaborators and as a meeting place for Europe's intellectual and artistic elite in that period.

Walter Gropius designed this building in Dessau, put up in 1925–1926, to house the Bauhaus art, design and architecture school. Its wings, framed in reinforced concrete, spread across a flat site, so the building lacks a 'front' in the usual sense. Because the support columns are set back from the edge, Gropius could stretch an unbroken glass facade over all three floors along the building's full length. That delicate steel-framed glass skin also caused major problems with sun protection and with controlling the indoor climate. The building was restored and partly modernised in 1976, then restored and repaired again between 1996 and 2006 following the principles of historic preservation. Since 1996 it has formed part of Bauhaus and its Sites, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Designed by the Japanese firm SANAA, this urban campus in Milan extends Bocconi University. It contains a new home for SDA Bocconi School of Management, a dormitory for students and a sports centre with an Olympic-size pool. Sinuous volumes and facades, glazing at ground level and inner courtyards mark the buildings; these features, typical of architecture in Milan, make them porous to the public. Gardens lie between the buildings, and sheltered porticoes connect them, giving a covered route across the gardens. Together, curving forms, glass-fronted ground floors, inner courtyards and covered porticoes make up the main elements of the design.

Opened in May 1995, Phoenix's Burton Barr Central Library is a five-storey building of 280,000 square feet, designed by Will Bruder working together with DWL Architects. An open core in the middle holds three high-speed elevators along with a grand staircase rising five levels, called the 'crystal canyon', which takes people up through the building. The roof structure takes its cue from the tensegrity structures of Buckminster Fuller. Each of the two main facades responds to the sun in its own way: the north side has shade sails, while motorised louvres on the south side control the sun better. At solar noon, circles of sunlight from some of the roof skylights fall straight along the library's north-south midline, and a few reach the ground-floor lobby.

Nicholas Grimshaw's Eden Project lies in a former china clay pit at Bodelva, now reclaimed. Two vast enclosures, each formed from adjoining domes, dominate the complex and between them hold thousands of plant species; each imitates a natural biome. The biomes consist of hundreds of inflated hexagonal and pentagonal cells of ethylene tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE), held up by geodesic domes made of steel tubes. The idea for the project goes back to 1996, and building started in 1998. Heavy rain slowed the work during the first months, and because the pit lies 15 metres below the water table, parts of it flooded. Every planted space is enclosed by inflated cells on a frame of steel tubing.

From 1968 to 1978 Carlo Scarpa worked on the Brion Cemetery in San Vito d'Altivole, an L-shaped addition of around 2,000 square metres to the municipal cemetery next to it. Onorina Tomasin-Brion commissioned it in 1969; she was the widow of Giuseppe Brion, who founded the Brionvega company. Scarpa held that 'the place for the dead is a garden', and the sanctuary is laid out as concrete buildings with distinctive details among gardens and water features. Its influences come in layers. Venetian ones include gold tiles of the kind known from Byzantine mosaics, while the chapel draws on the Japanese tea room. Scarpa himself lies buried beside the Brion sanctuary. Conservation work restoring the Brion tomb was finished in September 2021.

Designed by mpART Architects (Min Hyun-jun), the Seoul branch of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art opened beside Gyeongbokgung on 13 November 2013. The museum was set up in 1969 as Korea's sole national museum for modern and contemporary Korean art, and today it has four branches: Seoul, Gwacheon, Cheongju and Deoksugung. The Seoul building sits partly on, and partly beside, the site of the building that once belonged to the Military Defense Security Command. Its design takes up the idea of the madang, or yard, to connect the building's inside and outside with what surrounds it. The madang also works as public leisure space and hosts outdoor art events and programmes. Inside, an integrated programme of contemporary art is shown together with Korean modern art.

Finished in 1987, Copenhagen's Paustian House ranks among Jørn Utzon's most significant works in Denmark. Utzon made the first design and posted sketches to Jan and Kim, his sons, who prepared the final drawings and building plans. The idea is explained by the image of a Danish beech forest: walking through one feels like passing along a hall of pillars that gives way to branches and a canopy of leaves, which the roof represents. Seen from outside, the building looks like a temple, framed by external pillars along the edge of the harbour. Inside, tall white columns with fan-shaped heads reach the ceiling, where geometric arches link them. Kim Utzon later added two neighbouring buildings, finished in 2000.

Robbrecht en Daem and Marie-José Van Hee designed the Stadshal, or City Pavilion, a large freestanding canopy in central Ghent, Belgium, built in 2012. It came out of a city project to renew the squares and public spaces of Ghent's historic centre. The canopy stands on the square between three older buildings: St. Nicholas' Church, the Belfry and the Renaissance Town Hall. Once built, it was criticised on three counts: its size, its height, and its use of modern materials in such a historic setting. It is a public roof standing on its own in the heart of the historic city centre.

Lilly Reich and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed the Barcelona Pavilion as Germany's pavilion at the 1929 International Exposition. It was intended to present the new Weimar Germany as democratic, culturally progressive, prosperous and pacifist: a self-portrait in architecture. Since it had no accommodation, Mies could treat it as one continuous space that blurs inside and outside. Structure and enclosure are kept strictly apart: a regular grid of chrome-clad cruciform steel columns carries relatively small roof plates, while freely spaced planes shape the space. Visitors are not led in a straight line but take continuous turns as they move through. The form is simple, the materials costly: marble, red onyx and travertine. Between 1983 and 1986 Catalan architects rebuilt it permanently, using historical drawings and footings rediscovered on the site.

Verona's Castelvecchio Museum, in northern Italy, is housed in the medieval castle that gives it its name. Carlo Scarpa restored the building from 1959 to 1973, improving how both the building and its exhibits look. His work is visible in details such as doorways, stairs, furniture and even fittings made to hold a single artwork. The renovation balances old and new with care, exposing the original building's past where that was appropriate. At the time the approach was unusual; it has since become common in renovation work. On display are paintings, sculpture and statues, ceramics, miniatures, gold works, ancient weapons and some old bells.

Dudhsagar Dairy, a cooperative dairy union in Mehsana, Gujarat, is officially named the Mehsana District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union Limited. Achyut Kanvinde designed its plant, which is described as a postmodernist brutalist building; commissioned in 1970, it was finished in 1973. A cooperative movement modelled on Amul began in Mehsana, organising rural milk producers and encouraging them to pool their resources. The union was registered on 8 November 1960, and on 2 April 1963 Mansinhbhai Pruthviraj Patel laid its foundation stone. The dairy has had a significant role in rural development through the cooperative movement and in India's White Revolution.

Built by Ammar Khammash in 2005, Feynan Ecolodge stands in Wadi Feynan on the western edge of Jordan's Dana Biosphere Reserve. It belongs to the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature and was Jordan's first lodge of its kind, created to bring economic opportunities to local communities and to fund the conservation of the country's wild places. In place of open-cast copper mining, which is no longer viable in Wadi Feynan and damages the environment, it offers a sustainable alternative. The lodge is shaped like an ancient caravanserai. Solar power runs only the kitchen, bathrooms and reception office; candles made by hand nearby light everything else. Water is drawn from local springs, the vegetarian food comes from within 40 km, and the staff are all local, local women among them, which is unusual in rural Jordan.

On the Islands Brygge waterfront in Copenhagen, MVRDV turned two seed silos built in 1963 into the Gemini Residence, converting them between 2002 and 2005. The name refers to the twin silos through Gemini, the zodiac sign of the Twins. The architects used the silos' hollow cores for stairs, lifts and hallways, and clipped the apartments onto the outside, each with floor-to-ceiling windows and balconies along its whole length. The two silos are joined on every floor, giving a plan like the infinity symbol. A Texlon roof over the two rotundas brings in daylight and creates a lobby as tall as the building. At the base the raw concrete is left bare to show the structure's history, and the overhang leaves a narrow passage between dockside and streetside.

Kala Academy is a cultural centre at Campal in Panjim, Goa, housed in a 1983 building by Charles Correa. The Government of Goa set up the academy on 28 February 1970 as the apex body for promoting and developing music, dance, drama, literature, fine art and folk art. Several kinds of space for these arts are gathered in the complex: an auditorium, the Dinanath Mangeshkar Kala Mandir, along with an amphitheatre, a black box theatre, an art gallery and a library. Beyond performance and display, the academy trains students through its own faculty and organises festivals, competitions, exhibitions, workshops and seminars on the local arts. Its future is uncertain: according to the Goa government, the structure cannot be repaired or renovated and may need to be demolished.

Swiss firm Herzog & de Meuron designed this parking garage in Miami Beach's South Beach area. It sits where the Lincoln Road Mall ends on its west side, at Alton Road. To revive that end of the mall, Wennett, who chose the architects, kept the existing building and added a garage of the same height beside it; he spoke with ten well-known architects before picking Herzog & de Meuron. Partner Christine Binswanger led the design, which has been compared to a house of cards: an open-air structure without exterior walls, organised around buttresses and cantilevers, with floor heights ranging from 8 to 34 feet. Some internal ramps are steep so they can span the taller levels, and drivers reach or leave their cars by lift or by a winding central stair. Architects and photographers now seek it out.

Le Corbusier designed La Cité de Refuge in Paris for the Salvation Army, his third building for the organisation, and it was built from 1929 to 1933 in the 13th arrondissement, at 12 rue Cantagrel. It was one of his first urban housing projects. The plan sets a single long slab of cellular rooms at an angle to the street, fronted by free-standing sculptural volumes that hold the shared rooms: reception hall, dining room and offices. The facade was designed as a sealed glass wall with forced air ventilation, but the system never worked properly and was hard to control. Pierre Jeanneret later oversaw repairs, a brise soleil added in 1948–1952 and new windows for the roof pavilions. France listed it as a National Historical Monument in 1975, and it was renovated from 2007 to 2016.

Francis Skinner and Douglas Bailey designed the Cranbrook Estate in Bethnal Green, London, together with their older mentor Berthold Lubetkin, who had led the way for modernist design in Britain during the 1930s. Terraced houses, workshops and a large factory made way for Mace Street, laid out as a figure of eight that picks up the diagonal lines of the streets to its north. Centred on that street beside Roman Road, the estate has six tower blocks arranged in pairs by height. Opened in 1963, the towers took their names from the towns and boroughs then twinned with Bethnal Green: Puteaux, Velletri, Alzette, St Gilles, Mödling and Offenbach. In 2009, residents transformed a run-down children's playground into the Cranbrook Community Food Garden, where fresh vegetables are grown.

Opened on 23 April 1964 as the New York State Theater, this ballet and dance theatre at Lincoln Center in Manhattan was designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee. New York State paid for it as its cultural contribution to the 1964–1965 World's Fair, and New York City Ballet has been based there ever since. The 2,586-seat auditorium has four main balconies, called Rings, plus a small Fifth Ring, beneath a gold latticed ceiling centred on a large spherical chandelier. In 2008 David H. Koch promised $100 million across ten years to renovate the theatre and fund an endowment. The reconfiguration added two aisles at orchestra level, while backstage works brought new stage lighting and a bigger orchestra pit with a lifting floor.

Built between 1954 and 1960, this residential building by Oscar Niemeyer in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, fills a triangular site where Praça da Liberdade meets Avenida Brasil, once occupied by the Dolabela Palace. Mountains around the city inspired its curved form, and horizontal concrete brise-soleil run across its face. Its twelve storeys contain 22 apartments in various sizes and layouts. The ground floor was left open to frame the Serra do Curral range behind the square, but later buildings now block the view. The design caused controversy in its day, as some people objected to private homes on a public square. Finished before work on Brasília, it was among Belo Horizonte's first modernist buildings and is now protected at municipal, state and federal level.

Opened on 5 December 2008 in Yinzhou District, the Ningbo History Museum presents the history and traditional customs of the Ningbo area. Its architect, Wang Shu, became in 2012 the first Chinese citizen to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize. The concept combines mountains, water and oceans. The first three levels form a single square base with the main entrances and offices, while the galleries above break apart, like the nearby mountains, into five smaller, sharply geometric sections. Stones and bricks salvaged from demolished buildings in the area were laid by builders, who were given some freedom, using the wapan technique; other walls carry cement-covered bamboo, with each wall's angle deciding its material. Reported to be the first museum to use large quantities of second-hand materials, it won the Lu Ban Prize, China's top architecture award, in 2009.

Richard Meier's Stadthaus stands on the Münsterplatz, or Minster Square, in central Ulm, Germany, and is used mainly for exhibitions of modern and contemporary art and of photography. Meier set out both to complement and to contrast with the Gothic style of the Ulmer Münster. Construction began in 1991, after a decision by the elected city council, the Stadtrat, and the building was finished in 1993. Its 3,600 square metres are spread over four levels linked by an open staircase that gives views into the building and out beyond it. The materials answer the setting: Spanish Rosa Dante granite clads the building, floors the terraces and paves the square, while the slope of the roof echoes the neighbouring buildings. In 2019 it was listed as a monument of special significance to national heritage.

Churchill College is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Cambridge. Richard Sheppard, Robson & Partners won a competition with 19 entrants, picked from a shortlist of four by a panel that included Winston Churchill. Sheppard's scheme is firmly modernist: brown brick walls, precast concrete lintels and windows framed in teak, softened by generous grounds, landscaped to Sheila Haywood's 1959 master plan. When the college was completed in 1968 it had nine main residential courts plus a central building holding the dining hall, buttery, combination rooms and offices. The chapel has been called a modern take on a Byzantine basilica: its Greek-cross plan is drawn in concrete beams and exposed brick, and eight narrow slits hold stained glass by John Piper. Chapel and central buildings were each Grade II listed in 1993.

Lillington Gardens in Pimlico, London, was built in stages from 1961 to 1971 to a plan by Darbourne & Darke, and it was one of the last high-density public housing estates London built after the war. Seven years before the collapse at Ronan Point brought the tower block's dominance to an end, it reached high housing density with medium-rise rather than high-rise buildings. Homes are grouped in a way that stresses individuality, with private gardens at ground level and on the roofs. Broad 'roof streets' planted with gardens, together with the high build quality, help it fit in with the Victorian terraces around it. The estate wraps around St James the Less, a Grade I listed church built in 1859–61. In 1973 the historian Nikolaus Pevsner rated it as easily the most interesting housing built recently in inner London.

Rem Koolhaas of OMA designed the Netherlands Embassy on Roland Ufer in Berlin-Mitte, beside the new government district; it opened in 2004. The brief called for a solitary building combining the security normal for the civil service with Dutch openness. OMA's answer mixes obedience and disobedience: the block's perimeter is completed, while the embassy rises as a solitary cube. Diplomats had often met informally in the hallway of their old building, so the new one centres on a continuous route that reaches all eight storeys. Offices, set along the facade, are the 'leftover' spaces once this route was cut from the cube; one stretch forms a diagonal void through which the TV Tower is visible from the park. The route also works as the main air duct for the offices. It won the Mies van der Rohe Award in 2005.

Tadao Ando designed Omotesando Hills, a central Tokyo shopping complex built in 2005, one of several urban developments by Mori Building. It stretches 250 metres along Omotesandō, an Aoyama shopping street that also used to be residential. It took the place of the Dōjunkai Aoyama Apartments, a housing block inspired by the Bauhaus, put up in 1927 following the Kantō earthquake of 1923. Pulling them down revived questions about how much interest Japan has in preserving its historic buildings. A small part of the old apartments has been rebuilt in the complex's south-east corner, so a fragment of the earlier housing survives among the shops that replaced it.

Arne Jacobsen designed this filling station in Skovshoved, on Copenhagen's northern outskirts, and it opened in 1936, an example of the period's typical functionalist style. Texaco commissioned it, Uno-X runs it today, and it still works as a filling station. An oval canopy that projects outward, popularly called 'The Mushroom', dominates the exterior. It gives drivers shade and shelter while they fill up, and when lit from below at night it also acts as a sign. The pumps and roof still serve the fuel trade, but the main building is now an ice cream parlour unrelated to the fuel business. The station is Class A listed and underwent a thorough restoration in 2002.

In 1967 Richard Rogers and Su Rogers, his wife at the time, designed 22 Parkside for his parents; it went up in 1968–70 on a narrow wooded plot facing Wimbledon Common, London. The single-storey house is built from steel ribs painted bright yellow, glazed full height at both ends. It has two parts: a flat with a pottery studio for Rogers' mother, and the main house among the trees behind. On two opposite sides glass runs from ceiling to wall, facing a courtyard and landscaped gardens. Rogers said its approach, such as prefabricated steel and glass modules, inspired much of his later work, including the Centre Georges Pompidou and the Lloyd's building. Described as an early built example in Britain of a steel-framed High-Tech house, it has been Grade II* listed since 22 February 2013.

Vienna's Academy of Fine Arts is a public art school. It began in 1688 as a private academy; today it is a public university with over 1,500 students and six institutes. Its main building is on Schillerplatz, near the Ringstraße in the Innere Stadt district. Theophil Hansen planned it as part of the laying out of the Ringstraße boulevard, and it was inaugurated on 3 April 1877. Work on the interiors went on until 1892 and included ceiling frescos by Anselm Feuerbach. The academy has held university status since 1998 while keeping its original name. It also houses an art collection open to the public, which includes Hieronymus Bosch's triptych The Last Judgement.

Built in 1981, Les Arcades du Lac is a group of apartment buildings in Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines, a ville nouvelle near Versailles outside Paris. Ricardo Bofill's Taller de Arquitectura designed this mix of suburban and HLM housing as the centrepiece of an urban composition; its central section, Le Viaduc, reaches out from the shore into an artificial lake. The Pont d'Avignon, the Aqueduct of Segovia and the Château de Chenonceau inspired the design. The critic Charles Jencks saw the whole project as an adaptation of Versailles, a 'Versailles for the people', and pointed to Claude Nicolas Ledoux's influence on how the elevations are detailed. Bofill wanted the new housing of the 1970s and 1980s to stand in contrast to the Le Corbusier-inspired housing of the 1950s and 1960s.

Lilly Reich and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed this house in Brno for Fritz and Greta Tugendhat, and construction ran from 1928 to 1930. The free-standing, three-storey villa sits on a slope facing south-west. An iron framework let Mies do without load-bearing walls and lay out the interior to feel spacious and light. The main living area has a curtain wall of large windows framing a view of Špilberk Castle, and two of them can be lowered completely into the floor. A wall of brown-gold onyx from Morocco's Atlas Mountains divides the space. Mies and Reich specified all the furnishings, including the Tugendhat and Brno chairs, and the house had air conditioning, unusual for its time. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001, it has been a museum run by the city of Brno since 1994.

Casa de Ferro, the Iron House, is a prefabricated iron building made in Belgium and put back together in Maputo, Mozambique, in 1892. The Societé Anonyme des Forges d'Aiseau produced it using the Danly system, devised by Joseph Danly, a Belgian engineer. Such buildings combine a wrought iron frame, cast iron pieces that join it, and thin embossed iron sheets that are decorative and structural at once. Panels fixed inside and outside the frame leave a clear space where air can move within the walls. No foundations are needed, so building and later relocating the house were simple and fast. It was never lived in and has served various institutions instead; popular belief blames the heat of the iron in the tropical sun, but research shows the Governor's wish for a more conventionally built building played a much larger part.

Paul Cauchie, an architect, painter and designer, designed this Art Nouveau house, built in 1905 on a plot about 6 metres wide at 5 rue des Francs in Etterbeek, Brussels, beside the Parc du Cinquantenaire. He and his wife married that year and decided to build there. Its facade stands out for allegorical sgraffito decoration, and it had a practical job too: Cauchie designed it to advertise and sell the couple's work, his sgraffito and her art teaching. At its very centre he wrote 'Par Nous — Pour Nous', meaning 'By Us — For Us'. The house exemplifies the Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art, applied to architecture.

Haystack Mountain School of Crafts, a craft school on the Maine coast of Deer Isle, moved to its present campus in 1961. Edward Larrabee Barnes designed both the campus and its 34 buildings, grouped on 8 acres of a property of over 40 acres on Stinson's Neck, which runs south-east from the island's main part. Barnes meant the buildings to sit comfortably in their surroundings and to open up views of the land and sea around them. In 1994 the campus received the Twenty-five Year Award of the American Institute of Architects, which honours work that has stood the test of time in both its construction and its original intent. In 2005 it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

SANAA's Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa designed this contemporary art museum in the centre of Kanazawa, Japan, near Kenroku-en garden. The building's shape is meant to keep its overall volume low, soften the project's scale and let people enter from several points. Its transparency serves a similar aim: to avoid the museum being seen as a large, introverted mass. Community spaces such as a library and children's workshop sit around the edge, with the museum spaces in the middle. The galleries vary in proportion and light, from rooms lit through glass ceilings to rooms with no natural light, and range from 4 to 12 metres high. Four fully glazed courtyards bring daylight to the centre. The architects wanted to pierce the galleries with windows, but the curators vetoed this, wanting each gallery to be more autonomous.

Le Corbusier and his collaborators designed this government compound in Chandigarh, India, conceived after the 1947 Partition, when Punjab's previously shared capital, Lahore, was lost to Pakistan. Across around 100 hectares it holds the Secretariat, the High Court and the Palace of Assembly, along with four monuments and a lake. Set at the northern end of the city grid with the hills behind, it symbolically crowns the city. Rough concrete is used for all three buildings, with brise-soleil and deep cantilevers, and the Modulor, a system based on human proportions, sets dimensions and sightlines throughout. Double-skinned roofs and deep brise-soleil reduce solar heat gain, and pools serve for cooling and rainwater catchment. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site along with sixteen more of Le Corbusier's works.

Chand Baori, a stepwell in Abhaneri village in Rajasthan, India, dates from the 8th–9th centuries and takes its name from Raja Chanda, a local ruler from the Nikumbh dynasty. Shaped like an inverted pyramid, it has 3,500 steps that descend 13 storeys to a huge tank at the base. No inscription recording the construction of the stepwell or of the neighbouring Harshat Mata Temple has been found. Rajasthan is extremely dry, and the stepwell was designed to save as much water as possible. Down at the bottom the air is 5–6 °C cooler than at ground level, and in spells of intense heat locals used it as a meeting place. Like many stepwells, it had religious and ceremonial roles as well as supplying water. In classical Indian writings on architecture, this design is known as a vijay vapi.

Oscar Niemeyer designed the Claudio Santoro National Theatre in Brasília as a multi-theatre building in the Modern style. This truncated pyramid is the largest building he designed in the city specifically for the arts. Construction began on 30 July 1960 and finished in 1966. Inside are three venues, Villa-Lobos with 1,407 seats, Martins Pena with 407 and Alberto Nepomuceno with 60, plus an exhibition gallery open to the public. On 1 September 1989 it was renamed after Claudio Santoro, a Brazilian composer and violinist. A long renovation began in January 2014, after irregularities were detected by the Public Ministry, and budget constraints kept the theatre closed to the public for a decade before it reopened in December 2024.

In Kuala Lumpur, the Malaysian Houses of Parliament are where the country's Parliament meets. The idea came from Tunku Abdul Rahman, Malaya's first Prime Minister, and in March 1960 the Public Works Department's British architect William Ivor Shipley was put in charge of the project. It was made known that the building need not follow Islamic styles, and the government left the architect free to design as he chose. The design was to put the tropical climate first, with air-conditioning. A grill-like double screen was planned for the facade, adding structural strength and helping to cool the building. The House of Representatives (Dewan Rakyat) and the Senate (Dewan Negara) sit in the main building, and members' offices occupy the tower. Tuanku Syed Putra Jamalullail officially opened the building on 2 November 1963.

Finished in March 2019, this 18-storey mixed-use tower in Brumunddal, Norway, stood 85.4 metres tall and was officially the tallest wooden building in the world until Ascent MKE overtook it in August 2022. Voll Arkitekter designed the tower for AB Invest, and the Norwegian company Moelven Limtre installed the timber structures, among them load-bearing elements of glued laminated timber. Stairwells, lift shafts and balconies are of cross-laminated timber. On the top seven floors, concrete slabs were used to meet comfort and acoustic requirements. Inside are apartments, a hotel, offices, a restaurant and shared areas, and a swimming pool occupies a neighbouring extension on the first floor.

The Pyramids are three 11-storey pyramidal office buildings in the College Park neighbourhood of Indianapolis, built between 1967 and 1972 for the College Life Insurance Company to a design by Kevin Roche. Roche's plan called for nine identical towers, so the company could add towers as it needed more office space, with no buildings standing empty. In each tower, two walls of reinforced concrete carry the unobstructed office floors and serve as L-shaped cores; the other two walls are clad in blue glass. With opaque concrete toward Interstate 465 and reflective blue glass toward the lake inside the complex, the buildings have been called abstract and sculptural. They rank among Roche's most notable works and played a part in his Pritzker Prize; in 2021 an AIA Indianapolis panel named them among the city's ten most architecturally significant post-war buildings.

Originally named Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy, Accor Arena is an indoor venue in Paris used for many purposes, chiefly sport and concerts, and it holds up to 20,300 people. Andrault & Parat designed it with Aydin Guvan and Jean Prouvé. The arena has a pyramid shape, and grass covers its sloping walls. On 17 February 1984 the Orchestre de Paris opened it under Lorin Maazel, joined by massed choirs, with the Grande Messe des Morts by Berlioz. During the 2024 Summer Olympics it hosted artistic and trampoline gymnastics, followed by the men's and women's basketball medal games for bronze and gold.

In the Sendling-Westpark district of Munich, the ADAC Headquarters is a high-rise office building that Sauerbruch Hutton designed after winning first prize in the competition; it was built between 2006 and 2011. The scheme stacks two parts: a five-storey base with rounded edges, shaped like an amoeba, and 18 tower floors above it. The facade is made of 1,152 elements in 22 colours that read together like a mosaic, and the palette was taken mainly from the client's brand colour. Besides offices, the complex holds a television studio, a printing works, a casino and a visitor and conference centre. On the same site, the historic Sander Villa was renovated with its original facade largely restored, and it now houses the library, archive and a conference room.

Of all Peter Behrens's buildings, the AEG Turbine Factory in Berlin's Moabit district is the best known. It was completed in 1909, with Behrens as lead architect and Karl Bernhard as engineer. AEG had employed him since 1907 as its artistic consultant, and he also designed the firm's products and logo. The hall is considered the first try at giving industrial buildings a restrained modern look. Its steel columns run the full 100 metres on the outside, plain, every bolt and joint on show; between them, vast windows lean slightly inwards as they rise. The gables are reinforced concrete, with the logo cast into one, and metal bands on the flanking piers make them look rusticated. David Watkin calls it a 'temple of power'; Tom Wilkinson, an 'up-to-date edition of the Parthenon'. A century on, it still makes turbines.

Named after Amos Anderson, a publisher and patron of the arts, Amos Rex in Helsinki is an independent, privately funded museum of contemporary art. JKMM Architects drew up the design, and the doors opened in August 2018. The aim was to join new and old: the galleries sit under Lasipalatsi Square, while the historic Lasipalatsi building keeps its importance above them. Asmo Jaaksi, the chief architect, said some link between street level and the rooms below had to be made. That link is a set of roof domes, which act as artworks and as skylights, so daylight reaches the spaces underground. The New York Times saw five conical domes rising from the square like upside-down craters on an alien moon. In the main gallery, ceiling discs hide the technical services and also shape how the room looks and sounds.

Homes and shops share one grade II listed complex at the Brunswick Centre, which lies between Brunswick Square and Russell Square in London's Bloomsbury. Patrick Hodgkinson drew it in the mid-1960s, working from studies by Leslie Martin, and it took the place of streets of run-down Georgian terraces. It started as a private scheme, when the UK saw few private mixed-use developments. Construction ran from 1967 to 1972, and the result was smaller than planned. Hodgkinson wanted the blocks painted cream, a typical Georgian shade, to honour the lost terraces. Too few private buyers came forward, so Camden leased the flats as council housing; the developer kept the structure and shops. After listing in 2000, renovation began in November 2002: the blocks got their intended colour, and the artist Susanna Heron added water features to the central space.

Named after Canadian National, the railway company that built it, the CN Tower is a 553.3-metre communications and observation tower in downtown Toronto, completed in 1976. The idea dates from 1968, when CN wanted a large television and radio platform for the Toronto area. The reflective new buildings in the city were reducing the quality of broadcast signals, so higher antennas were needed. The design evolved into a single continuous hexagonal core with three support legs that form a large Y at ground level. The main pillar rose on a hydraulic slipform, a platform that jacked itself upward as the concrete below set. Six elevators run in glass-lined shafts set into the three inner angles of the hexagon. For 32 years it was the tallest free-standing structure in the world, until the Burj Khalifa passed it in 2007.

Staff call it Edise: the Petrobras Headquarters, a brutalist office block in the Centro neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro. It sits on Avenida República do Chile, beside the Metropolitan Cathedral, and it is regarded as a landmark of Brazil's architecture. The Brazilian Institute of Architects ran a national competition for the building, and Roberto Luís Gandolfi's scheme was picked from over 200 entries. Openings in the facade link the interior with the outside while shading the offices from sun and heat. Roberto Burle Marx designed gardens both inside and outside the building, and the city has protected their original layout. In 2021, nearly half a century on, Edise had its first revitalisation, which brought in measures for sustainability and inclusion. The gardens are also due for renewal, with their original plan kept.

A Category A listed student residence, Andrew Melville Hall belongs to the University of St Andrews in Fife, Scotland. James Stirling designed it in the New Brutalist style during the university's large expansion of the 1960s, and it was built from prefabricated concrete modules. It sits prominently on the North Haugh, along a ridge looking over the St Andrews Links, and its form is said to recall passing ships, a theme common in Stirling's work. The geometry carries through to the bedrooms, which have irregular octagonal plans. On top of some blocks, glass enclosures shaped like garden greenhouses bring daylight into the stairwells. Construction errors meant decades of repair work, and plans for more buildings of the same design were dropped. DoCoMoMo named it one of its Key Scottish Monuments in 1993, and it was listed in 2011.

Offices, a hotel and apartments share De Rotterdam, a skyscraper on Rotterdam's Wilhelminapier. The Office for Metropolitan Architecture designed it in 1998, and Edge was the developer. Three linked towers, called West, Mid and East, stand on a common six-floor base; its bottom two levels make up a big glass plinth. Roughly 90 metres up, each tower slides a few metres off in its own direction, which helps the building resist wind and creates room for terraces. OMA first drew the towers fully apart.
