McArthur had been Wright's draftsman and asked him for help with the "Textile Block" system, and Wright spent four months advising on site in 1928; the blocks became a defining part of the hotel's look. Original linen drawings kept by Arizona State University's library, along with a 1929 Architectural Record feature, confirm McArthur as the architect. The main lobby above all recalls Wright, whose unit block design had appeared on four Los Angeles-area homes six years before. A stained glass design here, "Saguaro Forms and Cactus Flowers", began as a Liberty Magazine cover Wright drew in 1926.

By 2008 the earlier building on this Tokyo site had decayed, and Kengo Kuma won the contest for its successor. He thought of the nagaya houses of Edo-period Tokyo and piled modern versions of those dwellings on one another, seeking an uneven void between floors. Architizer likened the steel-based result to separate wooden buildings stacked at different angles. The voids hold technical equipment; Kuma said he hoped to make people re-think the habit of assuming floors must be flat. Japanese cedar and glass dominate outside, recalling traditional Japanese architecture with a contemporary twist. An atrium joins the first and second floors, and on the sixth the sloping roof forms a stepped theatre. Planned at 41.3 m, the center was cut to 38.9 m when the city's assembly worried about the surrounding scenery. It won a 2012 Good Design Award.

Beneath the hilltop Albert Park in central Auckland, this gallery was founded in 1888 as New Zealand's first permanent art gallery. Its original home, built of brick and plaster in the manner of the early French Renaissance, was finished in 1887 and extended in 1916. At first the building also held the Auckland public library, and the gallery started out with collections given by Governor Sir George Grey and by James Tannock Mackelvie. In the late 2000s a proposed major extension met heavy criticism in some quarters over its cost, its design and the need to take land from Albert Park. The 2011 expansion, by the Australian firm FJMT working with Auckland-based Archimedia, raised exhibition space by half, with room for as many as 900 artworks, and added dedicated spaces for education, children and families.

H. H. Richardson designed this Harvard Law School classroom building, raised in 1882–1884 in the Romanesque Revival style. It was the first building made on purpose for an American law school, and the school's first home of its own. A heavy two-storey centre is flanked by single-storey wings, and the reading room runs back from it so the plan forms a T. The entrance, framed by a Romanesque triple arch, sits deep in the flat front, beside an off-centre stair tower that pushes forward. Longmeadow sandstone clads the walls in polychrome patterns, pale stones making checkerboards on dark, reddish surfaces. The three big first-floor classrooms suited Dean Christopher Columbus Langdell's new curriculum of large core classes taught by the Socratic method. The reading room is admired for its ornamented fireplace and its tie beams carved with dragon and boar heads.

Built in Brussels in 1893, this was the first house Victor Horta designed in the Art Nouveau style, a key step in the Belgian architect's development. On a tight budget, the family wanted a simple but comfortable home, and many of the made-to-order details of Horta's other town houses were left out. Still, every typical Art Nouveau trait appears: slender iron columns on the front, sgraffito, stained glass and mosaics, plant-inspired ornament and close attention to natural light. The decoration was new in making no reference to earlier styles, yet the plan stayed fairly traditional. Of three rooms in a row, only the first and last had windows, so the middle one, mostly used for dining, was rather gloomy. The municipality of Schaerbeek bought it in the 1990s; thoroughly renovated, it is now open to the public.

Two architects, Uglješa Bogunović and Slobodan Janjić, designed this Belgrade tower with the engineer Milan Krstić, and it was finished in 1965. It was the world's only tower whose cross section was a triangle with three equal sides, and one of very few that stood on legs instead of rising straight out of the ground. Those legs made a tripod, a symbol drawn from the Serbian three-legged chair, the tronožac. An enclosed observation deck took up the height from 102 to 135 m (335–443 ft); people entered it at 122 m (400 ft), carried up by two fast lifts. Though the work was high-risk, no worker was hurt or killed, rare for a project of that size. NATO bombing of Yugoslavia destroyed the original tower on 29 April 1999, and reconstruction began on 21 December 2006.

This complex in Hamadan honours the Persian polymath Avicenna. Beside a library and a small museum it has a spindle-shaped tower 28 metres (92 ft) tall, inspired by the Kavus Tower of the Ziyarid era. Houshang Seyhoun won the competitions for both this mausoleum and Ferdowsi's before leaving for France. A grand ceremony dedicated it in May 1954, timed for the thousandth anniversary of the philosopher's birth, and the avenue in front was renamed after Avicenna too. Since the Pahlavi government had built the monument, it was at risk of being defaced; yet because Khomeini admired Avicenna, the square kept its name after the 1979 Revolution. Listed as part of Iran's national heritage on 11 May 1997, the complex is now in the care of the Cultural Heritage, Handicrafts and Tourism Organization of Iran.

The Ayala Foundation runs this private museum in Makati, Metro Manila, which shows archaeological, ethnographic, historical, fine arts, numismatic and church collections. Fernando M. Zobel, a Philippine abstract painter, imagined it in the 1950s as a museum of the country's history and iconography. The Filipinas Foundation, the body now called the Ayala Foundation, founded it in April 1967. Its present home, a six-storey building of granite, steel and glass, came from the firm Leandro V. Locsin Partners under Leandro Y. Locsin Jr., whose father had designed the earlier museum. It stands where the original did; pulling down the old building drew some criticism from heritage conservationists. The new museum was formally dedicated on 28 September 2004, the Ayala Corporation's 170th anniversary, and after a two-year renovation it reopened on 4 December 2021.

Bahá'ís call this House of Worship, on the edge of Kampala, Uganda, the "mother Temple of Africa". When Bahá'ís in Iran faced a wave of persecution in 1955 and an earlier plan became impossible, two other Houses of Worship were announced, in Kampala and Sydney. A first design was turned down, and Charles Mason Remey drew a new one in Haifa, directed by Shoghi Effendi; it was approved in August 1956. Dedicated in 1961, it was the third Bahá'í House of Worship finished anywhere and then East Africa's tallest building. Italian mosaic tiles cover the dome and Belgian tiles the lower roof, while the wall panels have windows of German glass in green, pale blue and amber. Ugandan timber went into the doors and benches, and Ugandan stone into the walls. Against earthquakes, the foundation reaches 3 metres down.

George Chakhava and Zurab Jalaghania designed this Tbilisi building for the Georgian SSR's Ministry of Highway Construction, and it was finished in 1975. In the 1970s Chakhava was himself Georgia's Deputy Minister of Highway Construction, so he was both client and lead architect and could pick the site that best suited the design. The idea was to take up and cover less ground, giving the space beneath back to nature. A forest served as the model: the cores act as trunks and the horizontal parts as crowns. El Lissitzky's Wolkenbügel, the horizontal skyscrapers he designed in 1924, look very much alike. Its fair-faced concrete and sharp geometric volumes mean it can also be counted as Brutalist. The Bank of Georgia bought the building in 2007, and that same year it was made an Immovable Monument under the National Monuments Acts.

Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed this International Style library on Hewitt Quadrangle at Yale University, completed in 1963. A glass tower of book stacks, six storeys above ground, rises inside a windowless façade carried on four monolithic corner piers. The marble, from Danby, Vermont, was milled just 1.25 inches (32 mm) thick so that daylight seeps through in a soft golden amber glow. Bunshaft credited the idea to stone he had taken for onyx in an Istanbul palace, in fact the alabaster of the Dolmabahçe Palace hammam. A hexagonal grid of Woodbury granite veneer from Vermont frames the marble panels and is fixed to a steel structure. Height, width and length follow the Platonic ratio 1:2:3. Around the stack tower runs a raised public exhibition mezzanine, where one of the 48 surviving Gutenberg Bibles is on show.

Charles Correa designed this multi-arts complex and museum in Bhopal. The Government of Madhya Pradesh, through its Department of Culture, set it up and funds it, while an autonomous body of 12 members, the Bharat Bhavan Trust, runs it. Facing the Upper Lake, it opened in 1982, inaugurated on 13 February by Indira Gandhi, then Prime Minister. It brings together several art galleries, workshops for graphic printing and for ceramics, an open-air amphitheatre, a studio theatre and an auditorium. There is also a museum of tribal and folk art, along with libraries given over to Indian poetry, classical music and folk music.

Steven Holl won a 1999 international competition for this addition to the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City. With design partner Chris McVoy, he set five glass pavilions, called lenses, east of the original building by Wight and Wight. They crown the Bloch Building, an underground structure of 165,000 sq ft (15,300 m²). Placed at right angles to the main building, the addition was meant to engage the sculpture garden and join art, architecture and landscape in one experience. It houses galleries for contemporary, African and photographic work and special exhibitions, a cafe, the Spencer Art Reference Library and the Isamu Noguchi Sculpture Court. The plan was controversial during construction. It cost about $95 million and opened on 9 June 2007; that year Time magazine put it top of its list of ten best new and upcoming architectural marvels.

Boeri Studio, the team of Stefano Boeri with Gianandrea Barreca and Giovanni La Varra, designed this pair of residential skyscrapers in Milan's Porta Nuova district, both inaugurated in 2014. What sets them apart is planting: more than ninety species, tall shrubs and trees among them, spread across the facades. The towers share 800 trees, plus 5,000 shrubs and 1,500 perennials, hence the name, meaning "Vertical Forest"; the greenery helps cut smog and gives off oxygen. It also evens out indoor temperatures through the year by shading rooms and blocking harsh winds, and it screens the interiors from street noise and dust. Boeri has named a 1957 novel by Italo Calvino, The Baron in the Trees, as the inspiration; its hero leaves the ground to live out his life up in the trees. It won the 2014 International Highrise Award.

Sir Albert Richardson designed Bracken House, a late work of modern classicism, on a cleared bomb site southeast of St Paul's Cathedral. Its pink sandstone from Hollington, Staffordshire, nods to the pink paper of the Financial Times, set off by red brick, bronze windows and a copper roof gone green. Frank Dobson and Philip Bentham designed the astronomical clock over the Cannon Street entrance. In 1987 it became the first post-war building in England to be listed, at Grade II, rising to Grade II* in 2013. From 1988 to 1992 Michael Hopkins and Partners kept the old north and south ranges but swapped the central printing hall for glass and structural gunmetal on a Hollington sandstone base, its boxy oriels drawn from Liverpool's Oriel Chambers of 1864. The newspaper returned in spring 2019, after a refurbishment by John Robertson Architects.

Colin St John Wilson designed the new British Library with his wife, MJ Long, and no larger public building went up in the United Kingdom during the 20th century. Elizabeth II officially opened the purpose-built home beside St Pancras station on 25 June 1998. A broad piazza fronts Euston Road, with public art including large sculptures by Antony Gormley and by Eduardo Paolozzi, whose bronze takes William Blake's picture of Isaac Newton as its source. At the centre stands a six-storey glass tower, inspired by a similar one in the Beinecke Library, holding the King's Library: 65,000 printed volumes plus pamphlets, manuscripts and maps that George III collected between 1763 and 1820. Its reading rooms, eleven in all, began opening while books were still being moved in. The building was listed Grade I on 1 August 2015.

Ralph Erskine designed this long, unbroken block of 620 maisonettes in Byker, Newcastle upon Tyne. The site had held nearly 1,200 Victorian slum terraces, condemned as unfit to live in in 1953 and pulled down from 1966; the Wall and low-rise homes south of it replaced them. Design began in 1968; building ran from 1969 to 1982. The architects kept an office on site to build trust with existing residents. The tall block was meant to shelter the site from a planned motorway that was never built. Fairly cheap concrete, brick and timber were used, with bright colours and brick bands marking each floor. Its Functionalist Romantic style, with textured facades, coloured panels, care for context and modest height, broke with the Brutalist high-rise orthodoxy of the time. Fewer than one in five original residents ended up living there.

This large Edwardian city hall of 1905 stands in central Cape Town, on the Grand Parade, with the Castle to its east. It is built of honey-coloured oolitic limestone brought from Bath in England, and much of its other material, fixtures and fittings included, also came from Europe. A city hall was first suggested in 1887, around Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, as a tribute. In 1893, after the council had approved a scheme, H S Greaves, chief architect of Public Works, judged an open competition. The architects Harry Austin Reid and Frederick George Green won it, with T. Howard and F. G. Scott as builders. A turret clock in the tower strikes the hours and plays the Westminster quarters, and the carillon, with 22 added bells, was installed as a First World War memorial.

Formally the Transitional Cathedral, this building is the interim pro-cathedral of the Anglican Diocese of Christchurch, standing in for ChristChurch Cathedral after the 2011 earthquake badly damaged it. Shigeru Ban, the Japanese architect described as a "disaster architect", designed it without fee together with the local firm Warren and Mahoney, and it opened in August 2013. It takes its nickname from the more than 90 large cardboard tubes that make up its walls and roof. The A-frame rises 24 metres (79 ft) and stands on containers 6 metres (20 ft) long. It is built of cardboard, wood and glass. The site once held the church of St John the Baptist, the first that Anglicans in Christchurch built in permanent materials, demolished after the same earthquake.

San Francisco's third Saint Mary's Cathedral, finished in 1970 on Cathedral Hill, replaced the second, built in 1891 and lost to fire in 1962. The first options shown drew negative feedback, and the archdiocese then brought Pier Luigi Nervi of Italy and the American Pietro Belluschi into the team. The aim was a cathedral for very large congregations, where even big crowds could surround the altar, and a statement of God's presence, in beauty, within the earthly city. Its saddle roof is made of eight hyperbolic paraboloid segments, square at its base and forming a cross at the top. The building is 255 feet (78 m) square and 190 feet (58 m) high, under a golden cross of 55 feet (17 m). Some likened the roof to a washing-machine agitator and called it "Our Lady of Maytag".

Nicknamed the Balance Building, this brutalist exhibition centre marks the entrance to the Centro Administrativo da Bahia in Salvador, Brazil. João Filgueiras Lima designed it in 1974, chosen by Mário Kertész, then secretary for planning, science and technology. Its rectangular concrete body, 52 by 9 metres (171 by 30 ft), hangs 5 metres (16 ft) above the ground on cables from two matching towers at its sides. Each tower holds a cylindrical shaft 4 metres (13 ft) wide, one for stairs and one for a lift. At one end, an exhibition hall has a pyramid-shaped ceiling with a skylight; at the other, an amphitheatre turns that space upside down. To prove it was stable, the architect and Kertész stood beneath it as the temporary supports came away. By 2021 the building stood unused and in poor repair.

Alcoa commissioned these twin towers in Los Angeles from Minoru Yamasaki, and they were completed in 1975. With their paired arrangement, vertical black and grey lines and aluminium skins, they recall his original World Trade Center in New York. Each sits on an unusual triangular plan, and together they stand out as landmarks seen clearly across the Los Angeles Westside. Beneath them lies a parking garage counted among the largest underground garages anywhere, with room for roughly 5,000 cars. No buildings in California are taller except those in Downtown Los Angeles and San Francisco. On television, they were where two separate fictional private detectives of the 1980s kept their offices.

Set into the red rock buttes at Sedona, Arizona, this Roman Catholic chapel went up between 1954 and 1956. Marguerite Brunswig Staude, a local rancher and sculptor, commissioned it; the newly built Empire State Building had inspired her in 1932 to create such a church. August K. Strotz of Anshen & Allen designed it, with Richard Hein as project architect. Design began in 1953; seeing the site, the architects said nature had done everything and they need only understate. The main feature is a 90 ft (27.4 m) iron cross on the southwest wall, both decorative and structural. Walls and cross are reinforced coarse-aggregate concrete a foot thick, the walls sandblasted inside and out to expose the aggregate. Smoky grey glass at both ends cuts glare. The AIA gave it an Award of Honor in 1957.

New York architect Bruce Price designed the Château Frontenac in the Château style for the Canadian Pacific Railway, which built it. Opened in 1893, it was among the first grand railway hotels in Canada. It sits at 1, rue des Carrières, where Quebec City's old Upper Town ends to the east, on the raised promontory that pushes out into the Saint Lawrence River. The hotel has 18 floors and stands 79.9 metres (262 ft) tall, made higher by ground already 54 metres (177 ft) up. Terrasse Dufferin curls around it from northeast to southeast, looking over the river, and two public streets run through the building. It has been enlarged three times, the last major expansion coming in 1993. Canada made it a National Historic Site in 1981, and it is thought to be the most photographed hotel anywhere.

Les Choux de Créteil are ten round towers, each 15 storeys high, in Créteil, a suburb of Paris. Gérard Grandval designed them, and they were completed in 1974; the nickname, "the cabbages", comes from their oddly shaped balconies. The project began in 1966 on land that for a century had grown much of the vegetables eaten in Paris. The form was meant to be practical: living spaces sit nearer the windows, and the 2-metre-tall balconies give residents outdoor access and privacy at once. Those curved balconies were to hold ornamental plants and small trees so that the buildings would change with the seasons, but that part was never carried out. On 16 December 2008 the French Ministry of Culture recognised the group as "Heritage of the 20th Century", when it was seen as a symbol of 1970s French architecture.

Spread over 13.5 acres (5.5 ha) in Boston's Back Bay, where Massachusetts and Huntington avenues meet, this plaza belongs to the Christian Science church. Open space takes up 10.4 acres, along with a children's fountain, a reflecting pool measuring 690 by 100 ft (210 by 30 m) and six buildings. These include the First Church of Christ, Scientist, made up of the original Mother Church of 1894 and the Church Extension of 1906. When the site grew in the 1970s, Araldo Cossutta, working at I. M. Pei & Associates, designed three more, among them the 26-storey former Administration Building of 1972, now 177 Huntington. Church staff worked there until 2008, and it is now leased as offices. In 2011 the Boston Landmarks Commission named the plaza a Boston Landmark, noting how heavily the public uses it.

Frank Gehry designed this venue in the city of Concord together with the landscape architect Peter Walker, and it opened in 1975 under the name Concord Pavilion, with room for 12,500 people. Gehry came back to design its renovation and expansion in 1996, which brought more parking and more seats. The City of Concord owns the Pavilion, and Live Nation operates it. Its programme mixes concerts with local community events, among them a jazz festival held every year, and graduation ceremonies for the area's high schools.

CopenHill in Amager, Copenhagen, joins a waste-to-energy plant that makes both heat and power, called a new resource handling centre, to a recreational facility 85 m (279 ft) tall, in clear sight of the city centre. The plant began working on 30 March 2017. Bjarke Ingels Group designed the sports facility, whose sloping roof serves all year as an artificial ski slope, a hiking route and a climbing wall; it opened to the public on 4–6 October 2019. Made by Walltopia, the climbing wall reaches 80 metres, the tallest permanent one in the world. The chimney was first meant to release its exhaust not continuously but as rings of "smoke", really water vapour, but technical difficulties ended the idea. At the fourteenth World Architecture Festival, it was named World Building of the Year for 2021.

The Danish Maritime Museum used to be at Kronborg Castle. In October 2013 it opened in new premises by Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG), built around a former dry dock in Helsingør. Height limits set to protect views of nearby Kronborg led BIG to go underground, where the museum fills 7,600 m² (82,000 sq ft); the Dutch firm Kossmann.dejong designed the interior. The old dock, 150 m long, 25 m wide and 9 m deep (490 by 82 by 30 ft), suited the scheme well, though its walls had to be strengthened before the museum could be built around its edges. The dock itself stays empty, crossed by ramps and bridges that lead into the museum and its exhibitions. The whole is meant to feel like the deck of a ship.

Eero Saarinen designed the first two structures of this headquarters in Moline, the main building and the display building. His plans were approved in 1958, but he died soon after work began in 1962. The complex opened on 20 April 1964, with provision for linking more buildings to the south and west. Set in a ravine, the seven-storey main building is reached by footbridges at fourth-floor level, one leading east to the display building and the other west to Deere West, which Roche-Dinkeloo was hired to design in 1975 and which opened in 1978. Glass and Cor-Ten weathering steel clad all three. The display building holds a two-level auditorium and an exhibition area with Alexander Girard's sculpture mural. Sasaki Associates designed the landscape, with its two lakes. Its many awards include a Twenty-five Year Award honouring architectural excellence.

Finished in 1965, this federal tower in Downtown Albuquerque, New Mexico, holds both government offices and a courthouse. At first it carried a plain descriptive name; in 1976 it was renamed in honour of Dennis Chavez, who served for many years as a U.S. Senator. The Albuquerque firm Flatow, Moore, Bryan, and Fairburn designed it, having already done other local high-rises such as the Simms Building and the Bank of the West Tower. Its steel frame is faced in polished granite, and New Mexico marble lines the ground-floor lobby. The building rises 197 feet (60 m) over 13 floors above ground, with a basement and an underground car park below. In 2023 it was added to the National Register of Historic Places.

Ben Thompson founded Design Research (D/R) in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1953; the shop introduced the idea of the lifestyle store, selling furnishings by designers including Alvar Aalto, Marcel Breuer, Joe Colombo and Hans Wegner. In 1969 Thompson moved it to a new home of 24,000 square feet (2,200 m²) in Harvard Square, designed by his own firm on a block later known as "Architects' Corner". Its five storeys are flat concrete slabs on interior columns, wrapped in frameless tempered glass. Butting glass together without frames or mullions was unprecedented, and it let D/R be almost a building "without architecture". It was conceived as a glass showcase faceted like a diamond. Reviews were warm at once, one saying it pointed to a way of building in glass that could make a warmer city, adding colour, light and optimism to street life.
